"Abide" has three distinct meanings. Each one is important, and together they give you the full picture of this word.
Meaning 1 — To tolerate or put up with something

This is the most common meaning in modern English. To abide something means to be able to tolerate it — to stand it, accept it, or put up with it.

Here's the crucial thing: this meaning almost always appears in the negative. You'll almost never hear someone say "I abide this" — it sounds unnatural. Instead, you'll hear:

"I can't abide rudeness." → I cannot stand rudeness. It bothers me deeply.
"She couldn't abide the cold." → The cold was unbearable to her.
"He can't abide people who lie." → He has zero tolerance for liars.

The negative phrasing — "can't abide," "cannot abide," "couldn't abide" — is the natural, correct way to use this meaning. It expresses a strong personal intolerance. It's a step beyond mild dislike — it carries the sense of I genuinely cannot handle this.
Meaning 2 — To follow, accept, and respect a rule or decision (always used with "by")

When "abide" is followed by the word "by," it shifts completely in meaning. Now it means to follow, obey, or accept something — particularly a rule, a law, a decision, or an agreement.

"You must abide by the rules." → You must follow the rules without breaking them.
"She agreed to abide by the court's decision." → She committed to accepting and respecting the decision, even if she disagreed with it.
"Athletes must abide by the regulations." → They must respect and obey the regulations.

Notice the key nuance: abiding by something isn't just physical obedience. It means you accept it as binding on you. A person who abides by a court ruling isn't just grudgingly doing what they're told — they're acknowledging the authority of that ruling.

This usage is very common in law, formal agreements, sports, and professional settings.
Meaning 3 — To remain, to stay, to last (literary and old-fashioned)

This is the oldest meaning of "abide," and you will mostly find it in older literature, poetry, hymns, and the Bible — not in everyday modern conversation. Here, "abide" simply means to stay, remain, or endure over time.

"Abide with me." (a famous old hymn) → Stay with me. Don't leave.
"His legacy abides long after his death." → His legacy continues to exist.
"The memory of that day will abide forever." → That memory will remain forever.

You won't use this meaning in daily speech, but you'll definitely encounter it in classic texts, so recognizing it matters.

Though these three meanings look different, they all share a quiet core idea: staying with something.

In Meaning 1, the question is whether you can stay with (tolerate) something unpleasant.
In Meaning 2, you stay with (follow) a rule — you don't stray from it.
In Meaning 3, something simply stays — it remains, it endures.

Seeing this thread makes the word easier to remember across all its uses.

"Abide" sits on the formal or literary side of English. In casual conversation, people often swap it out for plainer words — "can't stand it" instead of "can't abide it," or "follow the rules" instead of "abide by the rules." But in writing, formal speech, legal language, and literature, "abide" appears constantly. Knowing it well gives you access to a wide range of English.

Don't mix up Meaning 1 and Meaning 2. The same word, used slightly differently, means the opposite kind of thing:

"I can't abide this rule." → I hate this rule. I find it unbearable. (Meaning 1)
"I will abide by this rule." → I will follow and respect this rule. (Meaning 2)

The presence or absence of "by" — and whether the sentence is negative or positive — changes everything. Keep that distinction sharp and you'll never confuse them.
